Consonantal i

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

nobody pronoun

also no one, no-one, not anybody, not anyone

classical

Varr. RR 2.1.2: nēmō enim omnia potest scīre
Cic. Fam. 7.30.1: scītō nēminem prandisse

nēmō, nēminis m. and f.

pronoun; in classical Latin gen. nūllīus, abl. nūllō

nobody, no one

Of persons only; for things, nihil (see nothing). Nēmō nostrum, none of us (see none); nēmō nōn, everybody (see everyone). Lewis & Short: classical Latin takes the genitive and ablative from nūllus.

Other words

  • nūllus, nūlla, nūllum — no (person); nobody, in the cases nēmō lacks

    adjective; gen. nūllīus, dat. nūllī · also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 3.4: et omnibus crēdere et nūllī

    Supplies the missing cases of nēmō (nūllīus, nūllō), and as an adjective agrees with its noun: nūllus amīcus, no friend (see no).

  • nec quisquam — and nobody, nor anybody

    nec with the pronoun quisquam · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 21: nec vērō quemquam senem audīvī oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset

    Where a sentence goes on with “and nobody”, Latin joins with nec and uses quisquam (see and not, someone).

Examples

  • nēmō enim omnia potest scīre

    for nobody can know everythingVarr. RR 2.1.2

  • ita Canīniō cōnsule scītō nēminem prandisse

    so, in Caninius’s consulship, let me tell you, nobody had lunchCic. Fam. 7.30.1

  • itaque nēmō adhūc convenīre mē voluit, cui fuerim occupātus

    and so far nobody who wanted to see me has found me busyCic. Sen. 32

  • Nēmō timendō ad summum pervenit locum.

    Nobody ever reached the top by being afraid.Publil. Sent. N 68

See also none, and not, everyone, someone, nothing, no.

SourcesLewis & Short: nemo · Lewis & Short: nullus · Lewis & Short: quisquam

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-varro, loci-cicero-epistulae, loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-seneca-epistulae, loci-publilius), checked against the editions named there.

Publilius is cited as the loci collection numbers him, by position under each initial letter in the Latin Library text; from N onwards that numbering differs from Meyer’s.
